reason: Whether the hypothesis variable exists is the central question here. Teams could easily treat any TERT row in the MAF as a promoter mutation, or miss that the assay may never have targeted the promoter.
text: Recurrent TERT promoter mutations (C228T at chr5:1,295,228 and C250T at chr5:1,295,250, hg19) lie upstream of the coding sequence in a GC-rich region that whole-exome capture usually does not cover. Before testing anything, check whether this study records TERT promoter status at all: look for Hugo_Symbol == TERT rows in data_mutations.txt, read each row's Variant_Classification (5'Flank/5'UTR versus coding) and Start_Position, and search the clinical tables for any TERT-related column. A coding TERT variant such as a missense mutation is not a promoter mutation and should not be used in its place.

reason: This is the central issue of the task: it decides whether the data can address the claim at all, and it stops activation from being read straight off a mutation list.
text: 'Pathway activation' is a functional claim, shown for example by phospho-ERK or MAPK transcriptional output. Before deciding, list every table and column provided (clinical, gene panel matrix, mutations MAF, SV) and check whether any expression, protein, phospho, pathway-score or functional-assay variable exists. If none does, finding ARAF N217I/G322S only shows that the mutations exist, not that they activate the pathway. Say explicitly which label the available variables can support and why.

reason: The key question is whether the comparison variable exists. Without this check a team could build a spurious comparison.
text: To test panel-vs-WES TMB correlation you need a WES-derived TMB (or WES mutation calls) for the same samples as the targeted-panel TMB. Before analysing, check whether such a variable exists: grep all clinical-table headers and '#' description lines for 'WES', 'exome', 'whole', and inspect data_gene_panel_matrix.txt and the mutation table's Center/Sequencer-type columns for any assay other than the MSK-IMPACT panels (IMPACT341/410/468). Do not construct a WES proxy from panel data; whether a genuine second assay is present decides whether the claim can be tested at all.

reason: Whether the exposure variable exists determines whether the claim can be tested at all, and using a proxy in its place would test a different hypothesis.
text: The hypothesis requires a community-level income exposure (e.g. census-tract or zip-level median income, area deprivation index) measured per patient. Before modelling, search every header and every '#' description line of all provided files for income, socioeconomic, deprivation, zip, tract, county, or other geographic identifiers. Do not substitute proxies such as race, smoking, PSA or disease extent for income. If an area-level income variable is present, model it with standard errors clustered by area (or a multilevel model), because patients from the same area are not independent.

reason: The deciding question is whether any response variable exists at all; without checking, teams may call True or False from prior knowledge.
text: A claim about uniform versus heterogeneous in vivo chemotherapy sensitivity of engrafted tumoroids can only be tested with a per-model response variable, such as treated-versus-control tumour volume change, mRECIST class, growth curves, or IC50/AUC. Search every column and every '#' description line of all six files for terms like response, volume, growth, IC50, AUC, mouse, xenograft, engraft, mRECIST, treated or sensitivity, and name the exact column used. Whether the hypothesis sounds plausible clinically (rectal cancer response is known to vary) is not evidence either way; the label must rest on what the data columns actually contain.

reason: Whether a subtype-defining variable exists in the tables is the deciding question for which label the task rules allow; teams must check for it explicitly rather than infer subtype from genomic tables.
text: SCLC subtypes SCLC-A, SCLC-N and SCLC-P are defined by RNA or protein (IHC) expression of the transcription factors ASCL1, NEUROD1 and POU2F3, not by any DNA mutation or copy-number change. Before choosing a label, list every file and column provided and search them (case-insensitive) for mRNA expression, IHC scores or a subtype annotation (ascl1, neurod, pou2f3, subtype). If such a variable exists, call subtypes per sample with a relative-expression rule (highest of the TFs) and report mixed ASCL1/NEUROD1 calls rather than forcing absence.

reason: If the direct variable is missing, building a proxy is the most likely way to reach an unjustified conclusion.
text: TERT copy number, TERT expression itself, IDH1-wildtype status or ATRX-wildtype status are not measures of TERT promoter mutation. Expression is the outcome, so using it as a proxy is circular, and the IDH/ATRX links are only correlational. If no direct promoter-status variable exists, any proxy changes the hypothesis being tested and can be reported only as context, not as evidence.

reason: Exact string matching on the protein change can miss or misidentify the variants. Presence or absence alone is easily misread as support or contradiction.
text: Find the ARAF variants by checking Hugo_Symbol==ARAF in data_mutations.txt and ARAF in data_sv.txt. Inspect HGVSp_Short, Protein_position, Transcript_ID, Variant_Classification, genomic Start_Position/codon change and the carrying Tumor_Sample_Barcode. Protein positions depend on the transcript; the canonical ARAF transcript is ENST00000377045 / NM_001654. If the transcript is non-canonical, match on genomic coordinate or codon rather than the 'p.N217I' string. Finding the variants is not evidence for the hypothesis, and not finding them is not evidence against it.

reason: This decides whether any test can be run at all. It also stops teams from reaching a True/False answer from ctDNA-versus-genomics associations that say nothing about anticoagulation or VTE.
text: Testing this hypothesis requires three things at patient level: a ctDNA-detected (yes/no) status, an anticoagulation exposure variable, and a VTE outcome (ideally with event timing). Before running any test, search every '#' description line and column header in data_clinical_patient.txt and data_clinical_sample.txt for terms such as VTE, thrombo, embol, DVT, PE, anticoag, LMWH, DOAC, heparin, apixaban, rivaroxaban, enoxaparin, warfarin, and for survival/follow-up columns. ctDNA status can be derived from plasma mutation/CNA/SV calls, but that alone does not make the claim testable. Do not use TMB, cancer type, mutation counts or other genomic features as stand-ins for VTE or anticoagulation. If the exposure or the outcome cannot be found, say so rather than building a proxy.

reason: Whether the measured variable exists at all decides which labels are possible. Teams need to check this first.
text: The hypothesis is about miRNA expression (miR-452, miR-766, miR-1180). The data are from a DNA-only targeted panel (MSK-IMPACT341): clinical, CNA, seg, gene panel and mutation files. Before any test, check every file for miRNA or RNA expression values (look for 'MIR'/'miR' rows and for any expression table), and check whether the panel gene list includes any MIR loci. Base the label on what you find.

reason: This is the most likely trap: a high correlation between two panel-derived TMB columns could be mistaken for evidence about WES.
text: MUTATION_RATE and TMB_NONSYNONYMOUS in data_clinical_sample.txt, and mutation counts recomputed from data_mutations.txt, all come from the same panel mutation calls (counts per panel Mb, with different filters or denominators). Correlating any of them with each other is circular and says nothing about panel-vs-WES concordance. To confirm, compute TMB_NONSYNONYMOUS/MUTATION_RATE per GENE_PANEL: a near-constant ratio shows they are rescalings of each other.

reason: Without this the comparator is easy to miss, which leads to a wrong 'Not verifiable' or to an analysis that never compares against established methods.
text: The established comparator is in the data. data_clinical_sample.txt has PROGNOSTIC_MODEL ('Genomic Risk Model Classification': Low/Medium/High), filled for roughly three quarters of samples. data_clinical_patient.txt has IPI (0-5), its five factor columns (IPI_AGE, IPI_LDH, IPI_ECOG, IPI_ANNARBOR_STAGE, IPI_EXTRANODAL_SITES) and OS_MONTHS/OS_STATUS. Count the patients who have PROGNOSTIC_MODEL, IPI and OS all present, and compare the genomic model with IPI head to head on them. Testing single genes against survival does not answer the question.

reason: The claim has two parts, and one part may not be testable with these files. Teams need to check this before they let a proxy variable answer that part.
text: The hypothesis has two parts: KIT mutation enrichment AND focal amplification enrichment in Triple_WT. Check the provided tables (column headers of all files) for any copy-number, CNA, segment or GISTIC field. Focal amplifications need segmented copy-number data; they cannot be inferred from point-mutation calls, and ABSOLUTE ploidy is a whole-genome measure, not a focal amplification. Do not use ploidy or mutation counts as a stand-in. In your reasoning, say which part of the claim the data can test and which it cannot, and choose the label by applying the task's label definitions to that.

reason: Grouping by the clinical column or pooling unmatched samples would give the wrong comparison.
text: Lesion type is not a clinical column: CANCER_TYPE_DETAILED reads 'Invasive Breast Carcinoma' for every sample, including JP and DCIS. Take lesion type from the SAMPLE_ID suffix (-JP, -DCIS, -IDC). Only patient JuP3 has a matched JP, DCIS and IDC. JuP1 and JuP2 have one unsuffixed sample each. The hypothesis is about JP versus its associated DCIS and IDC, so the main comparison is within JuP3 (JuP3-JP vs JuP3-DCIS vs JuP3-IDC). Do not pool the unmatched samples into a JP group, and state that one matched trio supports only a descriptive comparison.

reason: Whether the target population is present at all decides whether any ITH analysis is relevant to the claim. Teams have to check it first.
text: Before any heterogeneity analysis, confirm which cancers the cohort actually contains: tabulate CANCER_TYPE, CANCER_TYPE_DETAILED and ONCOTREE_CODE in data_clinical_sample.txt, and grep every file for 'renal', 'kidney', 'CCRCC' and 'RCC'. The library's inspection found only colorectal, small bowel and unknown-primary cancers (an IBD/colitis-associated cohort, with no CCRCC code). Check this yourself. Heterogeneity seen in tumours of other types says nothing direct about clear cell renal cell carcinoma, and the hypothesis is about ccRCC only.

reason: Whether the data can test the central claim depends on this; it decides what analysis is even possible.
text: Chromoplexy (chains of interdependent translocations and deletions) is inferred from junction-level structural-variant calls that give both breakpoint coordinates and orientations for each junction (the input ChainFinder-type methods need). Before any chain analysis, list the columns of data_sv.txt and check whether both sites have chromosome, position and strand fields, and count rows per sample. If those fields are missing, chains cannot be reconstructed from this table; say the chain-inference variable is absent rather than building an ad hoc proxy and calling it chromoplexy.

reason: This sets the evidence standard for the label. Without it, a team could read a high raw mutation frequency as significance.
text: Whether a pathway is 'significantly mutated' is a statistical question. The percent of samples with any pathway mutation does not answer it, because large gene sets made of long genes get hit by chance. Count the samples with at least one nonsilent mutation in the pathway genes and compare that count with a null model that accounts for each sample's mutation count and each gene's coding length (for example, permute each sample's mutations across genes weighted by CDS length, or run per-sample binomial tests and combine them PathScan-style). Make the call from the null-model p-value. A high raw frequency with p>0.05 does not contradict 'not significantly mutated'.

reason: This column is the most likely to be misread as drug-response data.
text: If data_clinical_sample.txt has a THERAPY_PRIOR_TO_DERIVATION (or similar) column, read its description line: it records the patient's treatment before the tumoroid was derived, not how the engrafted tumoroid responded in mice. It is a potential confounder of resistance, not a measure of sensitivity, unless a paired post-treatment outcome is also present.

reason: The hypothesis is restricted to MSS; the MSS definition and NA handling directly change the analysed cohort and can create spurious enrichment.
text: MSI-high colorectal tumours are mostly right-sided and carry BRAF V600E and RNF43 frameshifts (e.g. G659fs), so including them can make BRAF/RNF43 look right-enriched through MSI confounding alone. Tabulate MSI_STATUS (MSS/MSI/Inconclusive/NA) by PRIMARY_TUMOR_LOCATION in data_clinical_sample.txt and analyse MSS only. Many samples (about 327) have MSI_STATUS=NA but an MSI_SCORE; decide explicitly how to handle them (e.g. MSIsensor cut-offs: <3 MSS, 3-10 indeterminate, >=10 MSI-H) and report results both for strict MSI_STATUS==MSS and for score-derived MSS.

reason: This sets the logic of the decision. Teams often treat it as a frequency or exclusivity question and pick the wrong label.
text: The hypothesis is a universal negative: it claims no JAK2-nonmutated MPN patient carries a somatic CALR mutation. It is not a question about frequency, and the known near-mutual-exclusivity of CALR and JAK2 says nothing about whether it holds. Per sample, build JAK2 status and CALR status from data_mutations.txt (Tumor_Sample_Barcode joined to SAMPLE_ID), keep only MPN samples, and count samples that have a CALR mutation and no JAK2 mutation. One credible somatic CALR call in a JAK2-wild-type MPN sample is enough to refute the claim. A count of zero supports it only if those samples were actually profiled for CALR.

reason: Tells the team which kind of evidence the data can and cannot provide before they build an analysis around VAF.
text: Clonal selection means a shift in clone frequency (cellular prevalence), which normally needs allele read counts plus copy number and purity. The library reports that t_ref_count and t_alt_count in data_mutations.txt are empty for all rows; check this by counting non-empty values. If they are empty, do not claim that VAFs or prevalences rose or fell. Use what remains (mutations present in one sample and absent in another, and the copy-number tables) and say how much weaker that evidence is.

reason: This sets the criterion that decides the label. P-value comparisons are the most likely error.
text: To show 'outperforms', it is not enough for both predictors to be significant on log-rank, or for one to have a smaller p-value. Fit Cox models OS~IPI, OS~genomic model and OS~IPI+genomic model on the same patients. Compare discrimination (Harrell's C) and AIC, and run likelihood-ratio tests of the combined model against each single model. Outperformance means a clearly higher C for the genomic model, with a paired CI for the difference that excludes 0. Adding information beyond IPI (significant LRT) is a weaker claim and should be reported as such.

reason: If teams re-derive subtypes or keep the NA samples in the comparison group, the enrichment result changes.
text: data_clinical_sample.txt already has subtype labels in MUTATION_TYPE (BRAF_Hotspot_Mutants ~150, RAS_Hotspot_Mutants ~92, NF1_Any_Mutants ~28, Triple_WT ~46, NA ~43). Use these labels instead of re-deriving subtypes. Drop NA samples from both groups. Test Triple_WT against all other labelled samples and also against each subtype separately. State which comparison group you used. KIT is reported as roughly mutually exclusive with BRAF/NRAS/NF1.

reason: Prevents misreading missing measurement as a negative result about subtype presence.
text: ASCL1, NEUROD1 and POU2F3 may not be on the targeted sequencing panel used here; check whether they appear in data_cna.txt, the Hugo_Symbol column of data_mutations.txt and the panel in data_gene_panel_matrix.txt. A gene missing from these tables means it was not measured, not that the subtype is absent.

reason: The usual coding filter would silently delete exactly the variants the hypothesis is about.
text: Promoter mutations are non-coding and appear in a MAF only as 5'Flank (or sometimes 5'UTR/IGR/Intron) rows. Standard 'nonsynonymous only' filters (dropping Silent, Intron, UTR, Flank, IGR, RNA) remove them. Tabulate Variant_Classification for all NFKBIE rows BEFORE any filtering; this MAF contains 5'Flank and 5'UTR rows overall. Never conclude promoter mutations are absent from a coding-filtered table.

reason: Comparing unpaired pre and post frequencies mixes up acquired loss with tumours that were never amplified. Pairing defines what a selection event is.
text: Judge ERBB2 loss from within-patient pairs, not from unpaired groups. A post-trastuzumab sample without ERBB2 amplification shows acquired loss only if the same patient has a matched pre-treatment sample that is ERBB2-amplified. Pair samples by PATIENT_ID, using IMPACT_PRE_POST (PRE-TX / POST-TX) and sample-name suffixes (e.g. -P1/-P2/-M1a, -T01/-T02). Count the patients who are amplified pre-treatment and have a post-progression sample, then report how many of those pairs go from amplified to non-amplified.

reason: This stops the team from counting a race-only model as the race-plus-ancestry adjustment that the hypothesis specifies.
text: Self-reported RACE is a social category, not a measure of genetic ancestry. The hypothesis asks for adjustment for both race and ancestry, so look separately for a genetic-ancestry estimate (e.g. percent African/European ancestry, ancestry principal components). Do not report an ancestry adjustment when only RACE was used.

reason: This decides how the comparison groups are defined and whether 'no call' means anything.
text: In cBioPortal data, a sample with no mutation row for a gene is not necessarily wildtype; it may not have been profiled. data_gene_panel_matrix.txt contains samples with mutations=NA. Restrict any mutant-vs-wildtype comparison to profiled samples, and confirm that the genomic region of interest was covered by the assay, since absence in an untargeted region carries no information.

reason: Without a measured normal group, a tumour-vs-normal comparison cannot be made. Teams could mistake germline-control barcodes for normal tissue profiles.
text: The claim compares tumours with normal liver. Count the sample groups in the clinical table (CANCER_TYPE_DETAILED / SAMPLE_CLASS; the library reports about 9 hepatocellular adenomas and 10 hepatocellular carcinomas). Check whether any normal-liver sample has its own measured profile. Matched-normal (_N) barcodes may be germline sequencing controls only, not a comparison group.

reason: This sets the evidence standard for each label. Without it, a wide non-significant estimate can be misread as support for the claim.
text: The hypothesis is a null claim within a subgroup ('no benefit in ctDNA- patients'). A non-significant hazard ratio in a small ctDNA- group is absence of evidence, not evidence of no effect. Comparing p-values between subgroups is not a test of effect modification. If the variables exist, report the anticoagulation HR with its 95% CI in ctDNA- patients, give event counts, and run a formal ctDNA x anticoagulation interaction test. Support the claim only if the ctDNA- estimate is near null with a reasonably tight CI. If the CI still includes a meaningful benefit, describe the result as underpowered.

reason: These choices decide whether a real correlation test is valid and read correctly, if such a test is possible.
text: If genuinely paired panel and WES TMB values exist: use Spearman, or Pearson on log(TMB+1), because TMB is right-skewed and hypermutators dominate raw Pearson. Keep one sample per patient. Normalise per panel-specific Mb or stratify by IMPACT panel version. Keep correlation separate from agreement: panels can show systematic bias (for example higher TMB) and still correlate highly, and the hypothesis is about correlation only.

reason: This defines what kind of evidence could support or refute a universal ITH claim. It also stops teams from reading single-sample or primary-vs-met data as proof of homogeneity or heterogeneity.
text: Spatial intratumor heterogeneity is measured by sequencing several regions of the same tumour. With a single biopsy, subclones are missed and mutations look clonal. Count samples per PATIENT_ID (the library saw 171 patients with 1 sample, 3 with 2 and 1 with 3), and use SAMPLE_TYPE to check whether repeat samples come from the same primary tumour or are primary/metastasis pairs. Primary-versus-metastasis differences reflect metastatic/temporal heterogeneity, not intratumor heterogeneity. Because the claim is universal ('all tumours'), refuting it would require a tumour shown to be homogeneous after adequate multi-region sampling. Not detecting subclones in one or a few samples is not evidence of homogeneity.

reason: This defines the right unit of analysis. A pooled per-sample comparison answers a different question and could give the wrong label.
text: 'Acquiring new alterations' is a within-patient, over-time claim. Find patients with two or more samples (repeated PATIENT_ID in data_clinical_sample.txt; use SAMPLE_TYPE such as Primary vs Recurrence/Metastasis, or sample suffixes T01/T02, to put them in order). For each patient, count alterations present in a later sample but absent from the earliest one. Then compare these per-patient acquired counts between fusion-negative (FN) and fusion-positive (FP) patients. Pooled per-sample alteration counts or TMB do not measure acquisition.

reason: Stops the team reading an incomplete SV table as negative evidence.
text: cBioPortal SV files often hold only curated fusions (e.g. ETS/ERG fusions), not the full somatic rearrangement catalogue. Compare the number of SV rows with the number of samples and tabulate Event_Info and genes. If the table is essentially a fusion annotation, a lack of chains or few rearrangements in it says nothing about whether rearrangements are rare or unchained.

reason: Whole-exome MAFs can contain germline or artefact calls that look like recurrent drivers.
text: For the ARAF rows, check dbSNP_RS, FILTER, t_alt_count/t_depth (VAF), and whether the same coordinate recurs across samples. Germline polymorphisms, low-VAF calls and duplicated records should not be counted as somatic activating events.

reason: How the gene set is defined can flip the conclusion, so it needs to be fixed in advance and checked for sensitivity.
text: The result depends heavily on which genes define ERBB-PI3K. Write the gene list out. Use a narrow curated set as the primary test: EGFR, ERBB2, ERBB3, ERBB4, PIK3CA, PIK3CB, PIK3R1, PIK3R2, PTEN, AKT1, AKT2, AKT3, MTOR, TSC1, TSC2, RICTOR, RPTOR, STK11, INPP4B and PPP2R1A, which is the TCGA 2018 PI3K set plus the ERBB receptors. Then rerun with a broader KEGG ErbB set as a sensitivity check. If the two disagree, report the curated result as primary and note the difference.

reason: This prevents a wrong 'Not verifiable' label and clarifies what counts as contrary evidence.
text: data_cna_hg19.seg contains segmented copy number for JuP3-JP, JuP3-DCIS and JuP3-IDC (and for JuP1 and JuP2), so CNA burden per lesion can be computed. The relevant variable therefore exists. If JP shows fewer or similar CNAs than its matched DCIS/IDC, that counts as evidence against the hypothesis, not as grounds for 'Not verifiable'.

reason: The data are mostly genomic, so teams may be tempted to use genomic diversity as a proxy for response.
text: Genomic heterogeneity between tumoroids (mutations, CNA, TMB) is not a measure of chemotherapy sensitivity; genotype-to-chemo-response links are weak. An argument built only from data_mutations, data_cna or TMB is indirect evidence about drug response and should not by itself be used to call the sensitivity claim supported or contradicted.

reason: Defines the correct population (metastatic) and the exposure variable (sidedness); both are easy to get wrong.
text: The hypothesis concerns metastatic CRC, but the cohort includes MCRC_TYPE='Early Stage Primary' samples (about 123) and about 14 samples with PRIMARY_TUMOR_LOCATION=NA. Tabulate MCRC_TYPE and PRIMARY_TUMOR_LOCATION; run the main analysis on mCRC samples (mCRC Primary + mCRC Metastasis) with known Left/Right side, and include early-stage samples only as a sensitivity analysis. Standard convention: right = caecum to transverse colon (proximal to splenic flexure), left = splenic flexure to rectum. Check PRIMARY_SITE against the provided Right/Left label; transverse colon handling varies and rectum may behave differently from left colon.

reason: A filter that keeps only SNVs or missense calls makes CALR mutations look absent, which biases the result toward the hypothesis.
text: CALR driver mutations are frameshift indels in exon 9. Type 1 is a 52-bp deletion (p.L367fs*46) and type 2 is a 5-bp TTGTC insertion (p.K385fs*47), and there are many rarer +1 frameshift variants. Exon 9 lies at about chr19:13054500-13055000 on GRCh37. For all Hugo_Symbol==CALR rows, tabulate Variant_Classification, Variant_Type and HGVSp. Do not filter to SNVs or missense calls, or to one protein change, because that misses these mutations. Count every exon 9 frameshift.

reason: Defines the right comparison unit. Mixing in later passages or xenograft-only patients would test a different claim.
text: The hypothesis is about INITIAL engraftment, meaning patient tumour (T) to the first xenograft passage. List the patients that have both a T sample and an early X sample (X0/X1 or the earliest available) on the same platform. Some patients (e.g. SA429, SA496) reportedly have xenograft samples only. Keep changes at later passages separate, because they answer a different question. Look for any variable that marks primary versus metastatic origin. If none exists, say so and judge the general claim on the pairs you have.

reason: Unpaired comparisons on different subsets give results that cannot be interpreted.
text: IPI and PROGNOSTIC_MODEL are missing for different patients. Compute every comparison on the intersection of patients with both predictors and valid OS. Get a paired CI for the difference in C by bootstrap, or with survival::concordance on both fits together. A C-index or p-value from different patient sets cannot be compared.

reason: Counting non-coding WGS calls inflates KIT frequencies in every subtype, and with a file this large the analysis needs to be run in chunks.
text: data_mutations.txt (274 MB, WGS) contains non-coding and silent variants (Intron, IGR, UTR, Flank, RNA, Silent). When counting KIT mutations, keep only non-silent coding classes: Missense, Nonsense, Frame_Shift_Del/Ins, In_Frame_Del/Ins, Splice_Site, Translation_Start_Site, Nonstop. Count each sample at most once per gene. Read the file in chunks with usecols.

reason: Stops teams from using a weak genomic proxy as if it measured subtype.
text: MYC-family amplification (MYCL, MYC, MYCN) is only loosely associated with SCLC subtypes, and most SCLCs carry none, so CNA cannot assign or exclude a subtype for a sample. If tabulated, treat it as indirect context only, not as grounds for a True/False label.

reason: Matching on the gene symbol alone can miss promoter variants that VEP labelled with another gene.
text: Find NFKBIE variants by more than Hugo_Symbol. vcf2maf/VEP assigns each variant one gene, so a variant upstream of NFKBIE may carry a neighbouring gene's symbol; grep the all_effects column for NFKBIE. Entrez_Gene_Id is 0 throughout this MAF, and NFKBIE has the alias IKBE, so also match on SYMBOL, the Gene (ENSG) column, and a case-insensitive whole-line grep. Also select by genomic window: GRCh37 chr6, NFKBIE is on the minus strand, so its promoter lies at coordinates ABOVE the gene end (take gene coordinates from the MAF's own NFKBIE rows).

reason: This sets the population that the hypothesis is actually about. Including primary non-responders or samples taken before progression would dilute or distort any association.
text: Acquired trastuzumab resistance means the patient first benefited and then progressed on trastuzumab, with the post sample taken after progression. Restrict the analysis to patients whose treatment fields (e.g. TREATMENT, DETAILS_FIRST_LINE_COMMENTS) mention trastuzumab, who had HER2_RESPONSE CR/PR/SD, and who have a POST-TX sample. Confirm progression with HER2_TTP_ON_1ST_LINE_MONTHS and HER2_TX_STATUS. Exclude primary-refractory cases (best response POD) or analyse them separately, and state how many were excluded and why.

reason: Calling 8q gain with a naive log2 threshold ignores purity, ploidy and panel coverage, so the outcome would be misclassified.
text: Use the curated 8Q_ARM column in data_clinical_sample.txt as the 8q-gain outcome. If you recompute arm calls from data_cna_hg19.seg, use an arm-level rule (e.g. at least 70% of the arm covered by segments above about 0.2 log2), check agreement with the curated column, and prefer the curated column where they disagree.

reason: Using CNA as a stand-in for expression is the most tempting wrong method on this data, and it would lead to a label the data cannot justify.
text: Copy number (gene-level CNA calls or seg.mean over the miRNA loci) predicts miRNA expression only weakly and unevenly. The IMPACT341 panel does not target these miRNA loci, so seg values there are interpolated from sparse probes. The groups are also tiny (about 9 vs 10), so a proxy test has little power, and running several tests can produce false positives. Do not treat a CNA-based proxy result as a test of expression.

reason: This is the correct handling of the expression outcome if a valid mutation grouping exists.
text: TERT mRNA is low in abundance and often zero in RNA-seq, with a bimodal distribution across tumours. Check the fraction of zeros and the skew of the TERT row in data_mrna_seq_v2_rsem.txt. For group comparisons, prefer log2(RSEM+1) with a rank-based test (Mann-Whitney) plus a comparison of the fraction of tumours expressing TERT, rather than t-tests on raw values or on reference-scaled z-scores.

Before analysing, check whether such a variable exists: grep all clinical-table headers and '#' description lines for 'WES', 'exome', 'whole', and inspect data_gene

reason: If exposure is defined wrongly, a spurious benefit or harm can appear and flip the conclusion.
text: Observational anticoagulation use is confounded by indication (prior VTE, atrial fibrillation, high Khorana score). It is also prone to immortal-time bias if anyone who used anticoagulation at any later point is counted as exposed from time zero. Define exposure at baseline (the plasma draw) or as time-varying, and exclude or adjust for prior VTE and for cancer type/stage where these are recorded.

reason: This stops teams from reading raw panel VAFs as evidence of subclonal structure.
text: The samples come from targeted panels (e.g. FoundationOne; see data_gene_panel_matrix.txt and GENE_PANEL), which give too few mutations per sample for reliable subclonal clustering, and different panels cover different genes. If you try to infer subclonality from VAF within a sample, correct for purity and local copy number (TUMOR_PURITY, coverage, t_alt_count/t_ref_count, CNA at the locus) to get cancer cell fractions. If purity or depth is missing or inadequate, treat ITH as not estimable rather than calling mutations subclonal from raw VAF.

reason: This prevents a missense in a regulatory or kinase region from being inferred to be activating without a functional or downstream readout.
text: Background knowledge, not in the data: ARAF has low intrinsic kinase activity (non-canonical APE motif) and depends on dimerisation, so BRAF-hotspot logic does not carry over. reason: This is the most tempting substitute analysis, and it does not measure interdependence.

question: FINDING FROM THE LAB'S LIBRARY, asked for by the director. QUESTION: How is tumour purity or relative tumour content usually estimated from somatic variant allele fractions in whole-exome data when no matched purity tool output is available, and how strongly does low purity shrink log2 segment means and reduce copy-number calls? ANSWER: Purity is estimated as about 2x the VAF of clonal, heterozygous (monoallelic) somatic SNVs in copy-neutral regions, because these centre at VAF 0.5 in a pure tumour. TPES computes purity as observed VAF divided by expected VAF, using only SNVs in segments with log2R in [-0.1, 0.1]. PurityEst uses the mutant allele fraction at heterozygous somatic loci, averaged robustly per chromosome. CNVkit's documentation says the VAF of a clonal driver indicates purity. Copy-number changes at a mutated site and subclonality bias the estimate, so the median or upper mode of VAFs in neutral segments is preferred. Normal-cell contamination dilutes the copy ratio to (1 - p) + p*CN/2. A clonal single-copy loss is log2 -1.0 at 100% purity and -0.415 at 50% (CNVkit's worked example). A single-copy gain is 0.585 at 100% purity. The remaining values below come from applying the same formula: a gain is about 0.32 at 50%, about 0.20 at 30% and about 0.14 at 20%; a loss is about -0.23 at 30% and -0.15 at 20%. So below roughly 30% purity, clonal single-copy events fall at or under the common |log2| > 0.2 cutoff. Low purity can therefore greatly reduce both event counts and FGA, and can hide CNAs in a low-purity precursor lesion. HOW SURE: high. SOURCES: https://cnvkit.readthedocs.io/en/latest/heterogeneity.html, https://academic.oup.com/bioinformatics/article/35/21/4433/5490858, https://doi.org/10.1093/bioinformatics/bts365, https://cnvkit.readthedocs.io/en/stable/calling.html, https://www.keatslab.org/blog/dnacopynumberanditseffectsonlog2valuesandallelicratiosatdifferenttumorpurities.

question: FINDING FROM THE LAB'S LIBRARY, asked for by the director. QUESTION: In cancer-genomics literature, when a study reports that a lesion has a 'high number of copy number alterations', is that usually measured as a count of CNA segments or events, or as fraction of genome altered, and what log2 thresholds are conventional? ANSWER: Both measures are used, and the web does not settle which one a given claim means. One is a count of altered segments or events (segments with |log2| above a cutoff). The other is fraction of genome altered (FGA): the summed length of segments with |log2| above a cutoff divided by the length of all measured segments. FGA is cBioPortal's standard summary. 'High number of CNAs' literally reads as a count of events, but that is an inference about wording, not a documented convention. On cutoffs, |log2| > 0.2 is described as the conventional one for FGA. cBioPortal staff gave 0.1 in one help post and 0.2 in another. A cutoff of 0.1 is used as a lenient alternative (Spurr et al.'s AS/FGA), and CNVkit suggests 0.1-0.3 for gene-level calls. CNVkit's default call thresholds are -1.1, -0.25, 0.2 and 0.7. A comparison that holds only at the most lenient cutoff, or only with one metric, is weak evidence. HOW SURE: medium. SOURCES: https://groups.google.com/g/cbioportal/c/SqtGhn-AZ4s, https://www.biostars.org/p/406584/, https://www.biorxiv.org/content/biorxiv/early/2022/12/29/2022.12.28.522101.full.pdf, https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-024-68229-6, https://cnvkit.readthedocs.io/en/stable/calling.html.

text: FINDING: cBioPortal does not define or check the -2/+2 thresholds; it loads whatever integers the study supplies (-2 deep deletion, possibly homozygous; +2 high-level amplification). For GISTIC the high-level threshold is set per sample. For MSK-IMPACT-style panels, calls come from tumour/normal coverage fold-change with a cutoff, reported as about 2.0-fold for amplification in a source I did not open; the calls are typically not purity-adjusted unless FACETS is used. The diluted log ratio follows log2(p*CN/2+(1-p)): a 5-copy amplification gives a log2 ratio of 1.32 at 100% purity but only 0.81 at 50% purity, so whether a high-level call is made depends strongly on purity. Hu et al. 2020 report that metastases have systematically higher purity than paired primaries. No published rate was found for how often purity alone flips a ±2 call between two samples. Treat pairwise +2/-2 differences as weak evidence of acquisition. Confidence: medium on the mechanism, unresolved on the rate. QUESTION: What thresholds and purity adjustments define the -2/+2 calls in cBioPortal discrete CNA tables from panel log ratios, and how often does purity alone change a ±2 call? In a 427-patient qPCR-vs-NGS comparison, results agreed above 2% (the NGS detection limit), but 21 samples with qPCR burden of 0.1-1% were NGS-negative, and 1 of 298 with a qPCR burden of 3% was NGS-negative. MPN exome studies such as Nangalia 2013 NEJM ('CALR in MPN with nonmutated JAK2') define JAK2 status as a sample-level clinical category. text: FINDING: Yes, driver mutations can appear at low levels in T-cell or buccal normals. Nangalia 2013 NEJM used cultured T cells (34), isolated T cells (42) or buccal swabs (75) as constitutional samples. A PV exome study found apparent germline variants at COSMIC hotspots in PV genes in 7 patients, implying that pre-JAK2 clones contribute to T cells. An MDS study excluded T-cell normals with >5% myeloid contamination. The web pages read gave no single standard germline-read threshold. Commonly used cut-offs are normal VAF <2-5% (or a large tumor/normal VAF ratio). A CALR exon-9 frameshift with a high tumor VAF and a few normal reads should still be treated as somatic. QUESTION: When a scientific claim joins two components with 'and', and the available data can test only one of them, how do benchmark or fact-checking conventions usually label the claim: supported, or not verifiable/insufficient evidence? ANSWER: Fact-verification benchmarks (FEVER, FEVEROUS) use SUPPORTED / REFUTED / NOTENOUGHINFO. A claim is NOTENOUGHINFO when the evidence cannot verify it, and FEVEROUS explicitly asks for partial evidence on NOTENOUGHINFO claims. So a claim where only some parts can be verified is labelled NEI, not Supported. If the testable part is contradicted, the claim is REFUTED. No page I read states an explicit rule for 'X and Y' claims. The task's own definition of 'Not verifiable' (the data hold no relevant variables) is narrower than NEI and should take precedence over the benchmark convention. HOW SURE: medium. SOURCES: https://aclanthology.org/2021.fever-1.1.pdf, https://aclanthology.org/N18-1074.pdf.

question: FINDING FROM THE LAB'S LIBRARY, asked for by the director. QUESTION: In the genomic classification of cutaneous melanoma into BRAF, RAS, NF1 and triple-wild-type subtypes, are KIT alterations and focal amplifications described as features of the triple-wild-type group because of enrichment relative to other subtypes, or because of high absolute prevalence? And are triple-wild-type tumours over-represented among non-UV (acral/mucosal) sites? ANSWER: Enrichment. The TCGA paper says 'Integrative analysis reveals enrichment of KIT mutations and focal amplifications and complex structural rearrangements as a feature of the Triple-WT subtype', which is relative to the BRAF/RAS/NF1 subtypes, not high absolute prevalence. The TCGA cohort was cutaneous only, with all 67 primaries from non-glabrous skin, so acral/mucosal tumours were not part of that classification. Triple-WT tumours do carry the UV signature much less often: about 30%, against over 90% in the other subtypes. That figure comes from the Rajkumar & Watson 2016 review and I saw it only in a search snippet, because the page tool cut the text off before that section. UV status is therefore a plausible confounder. HOW SURE: high. SOURCES: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4580370/, https://www.cell.com/cell/fulltext/S0092-8674(15)00634-0, https://gdc.cancer.gov/about-data/publications/skcm_2015, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4947706/.

text: FINDING: In most clinical CRC sidedness series, the split is at the splenic flexure. Everything proximal to it, including the whole transverse colon, is right-sided. The splenic flexure and everything distal to it, including the rectum, is left-sided. The embryological definition instead splits the transverse colon, putting the proximal two-thirds on the right and the distal third on the left. Some studies exclude transverse colon tumours or treat the rectum separately. Loree et al. 2018 found transverse tumours cluster closer to left-sided tumours by mutation profile. They also found sigmoid/rectal tumours have less PIK3CA, BRAF and MSI than other left-sided sites, so including the rectum on the left tends to widen right-versus-left differences. QUESTION: Conventions for the transverse colon and rectum in CRC sidedness studies. SOURCE: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7505124/, https://aacrjournals.org/clincancerres/article/24/5/1062/81237/Classifying-Colorectal-Cancer-by-Tumor-Location, https://jgo.amegroups.org/article/view/89938/html.

QUESTION: In longitudinal multi-sample targeted tumour sequencing studies, how are 'acquired' (newly emerging) alterations usually defined when samples were not sequenced in chronological order (e.g. a metastasis sequenced before the primary)? Is ordering by collection date, by sample type, or by symmetric private-alteration counts the accepted convention? Acquired, de novo or metastasis-private alterations are those present in the later or metastatic sample and absent from the earlier or primary sample. Zhao et al. 2025 (MSK-IMPACT, 3,732 longitudinally biopsied patients) describe alterations 'emerging de novo' during metastasis, in the primary-to-metastasis direction. Hu et al. 2020 (457 paired primary and metastasis samples) and Ng et al. 2017 classify alterations as primary-private, metastasis-private or shared by sample type. None of them ordered samples by sequencing index. None used symmetric private counts as the definition of 'acquired'; symmetric counts describe discordance or heterogeneity, not acquisition. The defensible convention is chronological or clinical order: collection or procedure date where available, otherwise primary before metastasis. Re-ordering by collection date or sample type could change per-patient acquired counts wherever the sequencing index disagrees with that order. Only the Zhao et al. abstract was readable (paywalled), so its exact methods text was not checked. HOW SURE: medium. question: FINDING FROM THE LAB'S LIBRARY, asked for by the director. QUESTION: In cBioPortal-format discrete copy-number tables derived from targeted-panel log ratios, what thresholds and purity adjustments define the -2/+2 calls? How often does a ±2 call differ between two samples of the same tumour because of purity alone? ANSWER: cBioPortal does not define or check the thresholds. Discrete CNA data is loaded as integers from -2 to +2 as supplied: -2 is a deep loss (possibly homozygous) and +2 is a high-level amplification. In GISTIC the low-level threshold is fixed (about 0.1 to 0.3) and the high-level threshold is set per sample from arm-level values. Panel pipelines such as MSK-IMPACT call from tumour/normal coverage fold-change with a fixed cutoff, reported as about 2-fold for amplification in a search snippet I could not open. These calls are generally not purity-adjusted unless FACETS integer copy numbers are used. Purity strongly changes the observed log ratio, which follows log2(p*CN/2 + (1-p)). A 5-copy amplification gives a log2 ratio of about 1.32 at 100% purity but only about 0.81 at 50% purity. The CNVkit validation paper (PMC9302205) describes tumour purity as a variable that affects CNA calling. Hu et al. 2020 found metastases had systematically higher purity than paired primaries. That bias would produce apparent +2/-2 'gains' in the metastasis. I found no published rate for how often purity alone flips a ±2 call between same-tumour samples, so the web does not settle that part. Pairwise ±2 differences, especially without purity adjustment, are weak evidence of acquisition. HOW SURE: medium on the threshold and purity mechanism; the frequency of purity-driven discordance is unresolved (low). SOURCES: https://docs.cbioportal.org/user-guide/faq/, https://groups.google.com/g/cbioportal/c/qP_OaeRdbDo, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9302205/, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7343625/.

text: FINDING: Length-aware pathway tests build the null from random mutation in which each gene's chance of being hit is proportional to its coding length, and they work per sample. PathScan (Wendl et al. 2011) uses gene lengths with a single background mutation rate, scores each pathway gene as mutated or not, computes a p-value in each sample and combines them across samples with Fisher-Lancaster. PathScore uses a per-patient hypergeometric test that conditions on each patient's total mutation count and weights genes by transcript length times BMR, against a background of all genes in the pathway database. The Jia/Zhao weighted resampling method (PLoS One 2012) draws random gene sets weighted by per-individual BMR times gene length. Unweighted random gene sets are what these papers call the biased 'standard' approach: long-gene pathways come out falsely significant. question: FINDING FROM THE LAB'S LIBRARY, asked for by the director. QUESTION: In exome-sequencing studies of myeloproliferative neoplasms, how often does exome variant calling miss JAK2 V617F at low allele burden compared with allele-specific PCR, and do such studies usually report sample-level JAK2 status from a separate assay? ANSWER: NGS misses JAK2 V617F mainly below about 1-2% allele burden. In a 427-patient qPCR-vs-NGS comparison, the two methods agreed above 2% (the NGS limit of detection). Only 1 of 298 samples was NGS-negative at a qPCR burden of 3%, but 21 samples with qPCR burdens of 0.1-1% were NGS-negative. A deep NGS vs dPCR study (52 samples, more than 3500x) found 100% positivity concordance at burdens of 2.5% and above. Exome depth (~100x) is much lower, so exome-based calls would likely miss more low-burden cases. MPN exome studies (e.g. Nangalia et al. 2013 NEJM) classify patients as JAK2-mutated or nonmutated at the sample level. The pages read did not show which assay they used, so the 'separate assay' part is not settled by the web. Practical recommendation: if the study supplies a sample-level JAK2 annotation, use it in preference to treating an absent MAF row as JAK2-nonmutated. Also note that a missed low-burden JAK2 would rarely matter for a CALR-positive sample, because the drivers are near mutually exclusive. HOW SURE: medium. SOURCES: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30259120/, https://doi.org/10.1182/blood-2023-188510, https://www.nejm.org/doi/10.1056/NEJMoa1312542, https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa1311347.

question: FINDING FROM THE LAB'S LIBRARY, asked for by the director. QUESTION: When a myeloid neoplasm study uses a matched normal derived from T cells or buccal cells, can somatic driver mutations appear at low levels in the 'germline' sample, and what germline-read threshold is conventionally used to call a variant somatic? ANSWER: Yes. Nangalia et al. 2013 used cultured T cells, isolated T cells or buccal swabs as constitutional samples. A PV exome study using T-cell normals found apparent germline variants at COSMIC hotspots of PV-related genes in 7/31 patients, implying that early clones contribute to T cells. MSK paired sequencing found tumor DNA at VAF >2% in the normal samples of 25% of MPN patients. Buccal and saliva normals are known to carry leukemic contamination. An MDS study excluded T-cell normals with >5% myeloid contamination. The pages read gave no single standard germline-read threshold. Commonly applied heuristics are a normal VAF below about 2-5%, or a large tumor-to-normal VAF ratio, rather than requiring zero normal reads. A CALR exon-9 frameshift with a substantial tumor VAF and only a few normal reads should be treated as somatic. HOW SURE: medium (contamination of normals: high; specific threshold: low). SOURCES: https://www.nejm.org/doi/10.1056/NEJMoa1312542, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4532385/, https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-023-42585-9, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5969383/, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12672828/.

question: FINDING FROM THE LAB'S LIBRARY, asked for by the director. QUESTION: In colorectal cancer genomics, which oncogenic alteration classes does OncoKB assign to SMAD4 (missense in the MH2 domain, truncating, deep deletion) and to RNF43 (for example the recurrent G659fs frameshift), and is RNF43 G659fs regarded as a passenger linked to microsatellite instability? ANSWER: SMAD4: Truncating Mutations = Likely Oncogenic (Likely LoF); Deletion (deep deletion) = Likely Oncogenic (LoF); MH2-domain missense are curated variant by variant, with many rated Likely Oncogenic (e.g. R361H/C/G, D351H/N, G352E, G386D, R496H, R497H, W509R, G510R, R515G, D537A/E/G/H/V) and D537Y = Oncogenic. OncoKB lists 55 oncogenic, 4 inconclusive and 1 neutral SMAD4 alterations, and missense variants it has not curated are not automatically oncogenic. RNF43: Truncating Mutations = Likely Oncogenic (Likely LoF), and OncoKB notes they occur mainly in MSI tumours. However, G659fs*41 is curated specifically as Oncogenicity 'Inconclusive' (conflicting data), so under OncoKB it should NOT count as oncogenic even though it is a frameshift. G659Vfs*41 is a 1-bp deletion in a 7-G homopolymer repeat. It occurs almost only in MLH1-low (MSI) tumours, and Tu et al. 2019 showed the mutant protein works like wild type in Wnt inhibition. They concluded it is likely an MSI-driven replication-slippage passenger. A 2022 Nature Communications paper (snippet only, not read in full) dispute this and report a PI3K-activating effect, so the passenger view is widely held but contested. In an MSS cohort G659fs should be rare. HOW SURE: high. SOURCES: https://www.oncokb.org/gene/SMAD4, https://www.oncokb.org/gene/SMAD4/Truncating%20Mutations, https://www.oncokb.org/gene/SMAD4/Deletion, https://www.oncokb.org/gene/SMAD4/R361H, https://www.oncokb.org/gene/RNF43/G659fs*41, https://www.oncokb.org/gene/RNF43/Truncating%20Mutations, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6898356/.

question: FINDING FROM THE LAB'S LIBRARY, asked for by the director. QUESTION: In colorectal cancer sidedness studies, what are the usual conventions for classifying the transverse colon and the rectum (right, left, or excluded)? ANSWER: The most common clinical convention (most mCRC trial series) splits at the splenic flexure. Everything proximal to it, including the entire transverse colon, is right-sided, and the splenic flexure and everything distal to it, including the rectum, is left-sided (left = at least 63% of CRC). The embryological definition splits the transverse colon, with the proximal two-thirds (midgut) on the right and the distal third (hindgut) on the left. The rectum is hindgut and therefore left, but some studies describe the rectum separately (distal colon / proximal colon / rectum) or analyse colon only. Because the transverse colon is ambiguous, many investigators either assign it to the right or exclude it. Loree et al. 2018 (n=1,876) found transverse tumours' mutation clusters looked more left-sided than right-sided. They also found that sigmoid/rectal tumours have fewer PIK3CA, BRAF and CTNNB1 mutations and less MSI than other left-sided sites, so a large rectal share in the left group tends to widen right-versus-left differences for those genes. Splitting the transverse colon or putting the rectum on the left are both standard conventions; a robust analysis could check sensitivity by excluding transverse and/or rectum. HOW SURE: high. SOURCES: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7505124/, https://aacrjournals.org/clincancerres/article/24/5/1062/81237/Classifying-Colorectal-Cancer-by-Tumor-Location, https://jgo.amegroups.org/article/view/89938/html.

ANSWER: Length-aware methods define the null as random somatic mutation in which each gene's chance of being hit is proportional to its coding length, and they work sample by sample. PathScan (Wendl et al. 2011) takes gene lengths and a single background mutation rate (assumed not to vary between genes), scores each pathway gene as mutated or not, computes a p-value per sample and combines the samples with Fisher-Lancaster. PathScore uses a per-patient hypergeometric test that conditions on each patient's total mutation count and weights each gene by transcript length times BMR, against a background of all genes in the pathway database; it multiplies the per-patient probabilities. The weighted resampling method (PLoS One 2012) draws random gene sets weighted by per-individual BMR times gene length. These papers describe unweighted gene-set tests as biased, producing falsely significant pathways made of long genes. So the length-weighted, per-sample null is the standard way to define 'significantly mutated'. HOW SURE: high. SOURCES: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3106187/, https://manpages.org/pathscan/3, https://doi.org/10.1101/067090, https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371%2Fjournal.pone.0037595.

question: FINDING FROM THE LAB'S LIBRARY, asked for by the director. QUESTION: In random gene-set permutation tests for mutation enrichment, what gene universe is conventionally used (all genes with coding sequence, only genes covered by sequencing, or only genes observed mutated), and how does that choice bias the p-value? ANSWER: The convention is that the background must be the set of genes that could have been selected, meaning the genes the assay measured (for exome or somatic mutation data, the genes covered by sequencing, which is about all protein-coding genes). For genetic-variation studies a whole-genome background is considered suitable because every gene can carry a variant. A universe wider than what was measured inflates significance (p too small). An overly narrow universe, such as only genes observed mutated, deflates significance and conditions on the outcome. No source read supports a universe of only mutated genes. Neither source is specific to cancer-mutation permutation tests; they are general guidance for enrichment analysis. HOW SURE: medium. SOURCES: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8936487/, https://davidbioinformatics.nih.gov/documentation/tools/tech-gene-enrichment.html.

FINDING FROM THE LAB'S LIBRARY, asked for by the director. QUESTION: When a prognostic score with few levels (e.g. 3 groups) is compared with one with more levels (e.g. 6) using Harrell's C-index, how do tied predictions affect the C-index? Is collapsing the finer score to the same number of groups an accepted way to make the comparison fair? ANSWER: Harrell's C counts pairs tied on predicted risk as 0.5, or drops them in some implementations. That penalises coarse scores mechanically. With n equally sized discrete levels the maximum attainable C is 1-1/(2n): about 0.83 for 3 groups versus 0.92 for 6. Rounding or collapsing a score lowers its attainable C. So a raw C comparison between a 3-level and a 6-level score is tilted toward the finer score. Collapsing the finer score to the same number of groups is a reasonable sensitivity check for this tie artefact. It is not an established, standard adjustment, and a post-hoc choice of how to collapse adds its own selection freedom. The literature instead recommends likelihood-based comparison or continuous risk predictions. Give the tie-matched result moderate weight as supporting evidence, not decisive weight. HOW SURE: high on the tie mechanics; medium on 'collapsing is not a standard adjustment', because no source I read addresses the practice directly. SOURCES: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6041741/, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10219847/, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6996176/.

question: FINDING FROM THE LAB'S LIBRARY, asked for by the director. QUESTION: In prognostic-model validation, what is the accepted evidence that a new model 'outperforms' an established index: a difference in C-index with a confidence interval, AIC/likelihood-ratio improvement, net reclassification, or time-dependent AUC? How should results be judged when these metrics disagree? ANSWER: Methodologists treat likelihood-based measures as the primary and most powerful evidence of added predictive value (Harrell; Pencina, D'Agostino and Vasan). For nested models that means the LR chi-square test. For non-nested models, such as two different scoring systems, it means AIC or BIC. Comparing two C-indexes is a low-power, rank-based procedure that often misses real gains, and delta-C, NRI and IDI tests are degenerate under the null for nested models. A clear AIC/LR advantage alongside a small C difference whose CI includes 0 is therefore the expected pattern for a real but modest improvement, not a contradiction of it. Two caveats apply. A better likelihood does not by itself mean clinical significance. And 'outperforms an established index' is convincing only when the advantage holds after honest validation: optimism-corrected or external. Steyerberg et al. recommend reporting discrimination and calibration together. HOW SURE: high. SOURCES: https://hbiostat.org/blog/post/addvalue/, https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s41512-018-0037-2, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3575184/.

question: FINDING FROM THE LAB'S LIBRARY, asked for by the director. QUESTION: How large is the optimism in AIC and C-index when a risk classification is derived and evaluated on the same cohort, and what corrections (bootstrap optimism, cross-validation) are standard? ANSWER: Apparent, same-cohort performance is optimistically biased. The bias is largest at low events-per-variable and shrinks as EPV rises; bootstrap-corrected estimates match independent validation once EPV is about 20 or more. The size of the bias depends on the data, so the web gives no general number. The preferred standard is Harrell's bootstrap optimism correction, which must repeat every modelling step in each resample, including variable or group selection. 10-fold cross-validation is acceptable, and split-sample validation is discouraged. When groupings are chosen from the data in the same cohort, nominal p-values and effect sizes are badly inflated. Altman reports that minimum-p 'optimal' cutpoints give about a 40% false-positive rate, and a nominal P=0.002 corresponds to a true P of about 0.05. AIC's penalty of 2 per parameter does not account for that selection search. An in-sample AIC/LR advantage for a genomic classification derived in that cohort is therefore biased upward. Optimism could explain part of the advantage, or all of it if the margin is modest. Only a bootstrap that repeats the derivation, or external data, can settle this. HOW SURE: high on direction and standard corrections; low on magnitude for this dataset, which the web cannot settle. SOURCES: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5578404/, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5394463/, https://www.jclinepi.com/article/S0895-4356(01)00341-9/abstract, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2063091/.

question: FINDING FROM THE LAB'S LIBRARY, asked for by the director. QUESTION: In patient-derived xenograft genomics, what levels of copy-number and SNV discordance between the patient tumour and the first passage are usually attributed to technical noise, regional sampling or mouse-read contamination, rather than clonal selection? How is selection normally shown without allele fractions? ANSWER: No fixed threshold exists; the field uses empirical baselines. Woo et al. 2021 (Nat Genet, 1,451 PT/PDX samples, DNA-based): median PT-PDX log2 CN Pearson r = 0.95 (PDX-PDX 0.964); PT-PDX CN differences were comparable to multi-region differences within the same patient tumour; PDX-specific CNAs were not enriched for cancer genes. They read this as no systematic selection by the mouse host. Hoge/Ben-David 2022 reanalysed the same data with conservative 1 Mb-bin discordance calls and with ichorCNA, which corrects for purity and mouse contamination. They found a median of about 10% of the genome differentially altered (range 0-73%; over 25% in 24% of pairs) and call this real evolution. So differences of about 10% of the genome are contested, while large changes (over 25%) are more readily called evolution. Mouse-read contamination inflates somatic SNV counts (spurious private SNVs) but has little effect on CNA calls (npj Precis Oncol 2025). None of the pages I read gave a standard noise baseline for SNV presence/absence discordance. Without VAFs, selection is usually argued from: (a) recurrent or directional PDX-specific events, or enrichment of cancer genes among them; (b) divergence that grows with passage number; (c) PT-PDX distance above the multi-region or replicate baseline; (d) whole subclones gained or lost (the engraftment bottleneck in TRACERx PDX 2024, where models often carry a single subclone). Presence/absence or CN-state differences alone are weak evidence unless contamination is filtered and they are compared with a noise baseline. HOW SURE: medium. SOURCES: https://www.nature.com/articles/s41588-020-00750-6, https://www.nature.com/articles/s41698-022-00268-6, https://doi.org/10.1038/s41698-025-00902-z, https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-024-47547-3, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5659952/.

question: FINDING FROM THE LAB'S LIBRARY, asked for by the director. QUESTION: In circular binary segmentation of sequencing-based copy number, how do sequencing depth and the number of markers per segment affect the number of segments called, and what minimum marker or length filters are standard before comparing breakpoints between samples? ANSWER: DNAcopy segment() defaults: alpha=0.01, min.width=2 markers (the maximum allowed is 5), undo.splits='none'. The documentation recommends an undo option (sdundo with undo.SD=3, or prune) to remove change-points caused by local trends. Noisy or low-depth read-depth signals and outlier bins produce spurious short segments, so raw segment counts depend on depth and noise and cannot be compared between samples without smoothing or merging. Example: in the GATK tutorial, smoothing cut one sample from 638 to 398 segments; SAAS-CNV recommends merging adjacent segments whose medians do not differ. The pages I read did not settle a single standard minimum-marker or minimum-length filter. Practice is to merge or drop segments with few markers and compare samples on coarse bins (Hoge 2022 used 1 Mb bins) or on large CNAs (over 5 Mb in Ben-David 2017), not on exact breakpoints. Any specific numeric cutoff would be a convention, not a web-verified standard. HOW SURE: medium for defaults and the depth/oversegmentation effect; low for a standard filter. SOURCES: https://rdrr.io/bioc/DNAcopy/man/segment.html, https://gatk.broadinstitute.org/hc/en-us/articles/360035890011--How-to-part-II-Sensitively-detect-copy-ratio-alterations-and-allelic-segments, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4652904/, https://www.nature.com/articles/s41698-022-00268-6, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5659952/.

(3) As timeline files (data_timeline_treatment.txt with EVENT_TYPE TREATMENT). These record which treatments were given and when, not the response of each model. The study files the teams were given (clinical patient and sample, CNA, seg, gene panel matrix, mutations) include no Generic Assay and no timeline file. So if neither clinical table has a response column, the given data contain no response variable, and 'Not verifiable' is the likely label. question: FINDING FROM THE LAB'S LIBRARY, asked for by the director. QUESTION: In Ensembl VEP output, how is 'upstream_gene_variant' assigned (default distance window, relative to which transcript start) and what do the DISTANCE, TSL and BIOTYPE fields mean? Can a variant be upstream of one isoform while lying in the coding exon of the canonical isoform? ANSWER: VEP finds every Ensembl transcript near a variant and assigns a consequence to each allele-transcript pair separately. Ensembl states that 'each allele of each variant may have a different effect in different transcripts'. upstream_gene_variant (SO:0001631, 'a sequence variant located 5' of a gene', MODIFIER impact) is given when the variant lies within the upstream/downstream window, which is 5 kb by default (--distance; the REST API default is 5000), 5' of that specific transcript (the Feature). The upstream direction is set by that transcript's strand. Field meanings: DISTANCE is the 'shortest distance from variant to transcript' in bp, for the transcript in Feature. That it is normally filled only for upstream/downstream calls is my inference; the pages I read do not say so. BIOTYPE is that transcript's biotype (e.g. protein_coding, retained_intron, nonsense_mediated_decay). TSL is the GENCODE Transcript Support Level: tsl1 means every splice junction is supported by a non-suspect mRNA; tsl2 means the best supporting mRNA is suspect or support comes only from several ESTs; tsl3 means one EST; tsl4 means a suspect EST; tsl5 means no transcript supports the model; NA means not analysed (e.g. single-exon transcripts). CANONICAL flags the VEP/Ensembl canonical transcript. Can the case in the question happen? Yes. Because consequences are worked out per transcript, a variant can be upstream_gene_variant for an alternative isoform whose annotated start lies downstream of the variant, while it falls inside an exon (including a coding exon) of the canonical isoform. In that case the upstream label only places the variant within 5 kb 5' of that isoform's annotated start. It is not evidence that the variant sits in the gene's real promoter, especially when the transcript is non-canonical or has a poor TSL. To check, look at the canonical transcript's consequence (all_effects column, or HGVSc/Exon_Number on the canonical transcript). vcf2maf writes each variant to only one isoform, and all_effects lists every alternative. HOW SURE: high. SOURCES: https://useast.ensembl.org/info/genome/variation/prediction/predicted_data.html, https://www.sequenceontology.org/browser/current_release/term/SO:0001631/, https://github.com/mskcc/vcf2maf/blob/main/docs/vep_maf_readme.txt, https://github.com/mskcc/vcf2maf/blob/main/vcf2maf.pl, https://useast.ensembl.org/info/genome/genebuild/transcript%5Fquality%5Ftags.html, https://useast.ensembl.org/info/docs/tools/vep/script/vep_options.html.

label: FINDING
text: FINDING: Acquired-resistance association is usually tested by comparing alteration frequency in post-treatment/resistant tumours against a treatment-naive (or non-exposed) comparison cohort with a frequency test (e.g. Razavi 2018 Cancer Cell: 692 hormone-therapy-exposed vs treatment-naive tumours of 1,918, 'more than twice as common'), and/or by showing in paired samples that the alteration is absent pre-treatment and present at progression. When only a minority of resistant patients show a change, a control is needed: an untreated or non-HER2-treated paired cohort giving the background rate of the same change. For HER2 the background rate is substantial (Niikura 2012: 24% HER2-positive primaries had HER2-negative metastases, and trastuzumab exposure did not significantly change the rate, P=0.296), so a few recurrent ERBB2-loss events with no control do not establish association. Medium confidence. QUESTION: How is 'associated with acquired resistance' tested in paired biopsy studies, and what control is needed? SOURCE: https://www.cell.com/cancer-cell/fulltext/S1535-6108(18)30368-4 ; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3295557/ ; https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30806922/

label: FINDING
text: FINDING: The background rate of HER2 discordance between primary and metastasis is about 8-10% pooled overall (meta-analyses: Aurilio 8%, 48 studies; Schrijver 10.3%, 39 studies), with positive-to-negative conversion in about 21% of HER2-positive primaries. Single-centre rates of HER2+ primary to HER2- metastasis are about 24% (Niikura 2012, n=182; not significantly affected by trastuzumab). One study found that HER2 loss after neoadjuvant or adjuvant therapy was strongly tied to anti-HER2 treatment (47% with trastuzumab, 63% with pertuzumab added; Ignatov 2019). These rates come from IHC/FISH; no panel-NGS untreated-pair rate was found. For purity, MSK-IMPACT ERBB2 calls were 98.4% concordant with IHC/FISH, and the discordant calls occurred with low tumour content or HER2 heterogeneity. Amplicon NGS loses sensitivity for amplification below about 30% tumour cellularity (Oncomine). A non-amplified call in a sample under ~30% purity should therefore not be read as a true loss. Medium confidence. QUESTION: What is the discordance of ERBB2 amplification between same-tumour biopsies, and what purity is needed? SOURCE: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11420314/ ; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3295557/ ; https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30806922/ ; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5397722/ ; https://www.mdpi.com/2072-6694/16/23/3927

label: FINDING
text: FINDING: The reviews define selection of a pre-existing subclone as distinct from de novo resistance, and say it can only be shown if the resistant subclone is detected in the pre-treatment sample. Routine clinical assays often miss subclones because their abundance is below the assay's sensitivity limit or because of sampling. Showing pre-existence therefore needs subclonal evidence in the baseline sample, such as a subclonal or intermediate ERBB2 copy-number state, or heterogeneity by FISH/IHC. Multi-region or deep sequencing, or single-cell data, also count, as do shared clonal mutations that place the post-treatment non-amplified clone on a branch already present at baseline. Standard panel calls of amplified before and non-amplified after cannot tell selection apart from a de novo change or a sampling or purity artefact. The specific panel-based criteria were not set out explicitly in the pages read. Medium-low confidence. QUESTION: What evidence from panel data shows an ERBB2-non-amplified subclone existed before therapy? SOURCE: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5528620/ ; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4838548/ ; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5397722/

text: FINDING: Under the ClinGen/CGC/VICC oncogenicity SOP (Horak 2022), a non-hotspot missense variant is called oncogenic only by summing listed evidence codes: OS2 well-established in vitro/in vivo functional studies (4 pts), OS1 same amino acid change as an established oncogenic variant (4), OS3 cancerhotspots.org hotspot with >=50 samples at the position and >=10 with the same change (4), OM1 critical functional domain (2), OM3 smaller hotspot (2), OM4 different oncogenic missense at the same residue (2), OP1 concordant in-silico predictions (1), OP3 hotspot with <10 same-change count (1), OP4 absent from gnomAD (1). Likely oncogenic needs >=6 points and oncogenic >=10. Mutual exclusivity and co-mutation patterns are not criteria at all. Recurrence counts only at population-hotspot scale (cancerhotspots.org, or COSMIC/tumour-specific study for poorly covered tumour types), so a few cases in one cohort do not meet it. OncoKB rates hotspots from statistical recurrence alone as only 'Likely Oncogenic'. It records gain-of-function (activating) as a separate biological-effect call, and functional characterisation supersedes recurrence. So genotype and co-mutation tables alone can neither establish nor refute that a variant is activating; a functional or pathway readout is needed. QUESTION: What evidence is needed to call a non-hotspot kinase missense variant activating under AMP/ASCO/CAP and the ClinGen/CGC/VICC SOP, and can genomic patterns (mutual exclusivity, recurrence) alone meet it? label: FINDING
text: FINDING: Chromoplexy (Baca et al. 2013, Cell) is defined as chains of interdependent rearrangements (translocations and deletions) where breakpoints of different rearrangements lie near each other on the reference genome, often joined by deletions at the fusion junctions ('deletion bridges'), forming closed chains with little or no copy-number change. ChainFinder detects it by building a graph with rearrangement breakpoints from WGS junction calls as nodes and copy-number deletion segments as edges, then testing whether the connected breakpoints are statistically unlikely to have arisen independently. So junction-level rearrangement calls (coordinates and orientations) are required. Copy-number deletions are only a supplementary input that links breakpoints. None of the sources read gives a method that infers chromoplexy from copy-number segments alone, and because chromoplexy is largely copy-neutral, CN-only data cannot settle it (this last point is inferred, medium confidence). QUESTION: How is chromoplexy defined and detected, and can it be inferred from copy-number segments alone? label: FINDING
text: FINDING: TMPRSS2 and ERG lie about 3 Mb apart on chromosome 21q22, in the same orientation, so the TMPRSS2-ERG fusion forms in one of two ways that ERG break-apart FISH can tell apart. 'Translocation' (also called split signal, Esplit, or rearrangement through insertion) means the 5' and 3' ERG probe signals are separated but both are kept: the intervening DNA was moved to another place without loss, as in a balanced translocation or insertion. 'Translocation with deletion' (interstitial deletion, Edel) means the 5' ERG signal is lost: the roughly 3 Mb of DNA between TMPRSS2 and ERG on 21q22.2-3 was deleted, which joins the two genes directly. Edel accounts for about half to 60% of fusion-positive cases and is linked to higher stage and metastasis. These labels describe how each fusion formed. On their own they do not show whether a rearrangement is part of a multi-partner chromoplexy chain. QUESTION: What do the FISH ERG categories 'translocation' and 'translocation with deletion' indicate about how the fusion formed? SOURCE: https://aacrjournals.org/cancerres/article/66/17/8337/526226/TMPRSS2-ERG-Fusion-Associated-Deletions-Provide ; https://www.modernpathology.org/article/S0893-3952(22)02665-5/fulltext ; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2760294/ ; https://ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC1601467/

question: FINDING FROM THE LAB'S LIBRARY, asked for by the director. QUESTION: In paired pre-/post-treatment tumour biopsy studies, how is a claim that a genomic change is 'associated with acquired resistance' usually tested, and what control or comparison group is considered necessary when only a minority of resistant patients show the change? ANSWER: Usually by comparing how often the alteration occurs in post-treatment (resistant) tumours versus a treatment-naive or non-exposed comparison cohort, using a frequency test. For example, Razavi 2018 compared 692 hormone-therapy-exposed tumours with treatment-naive ones and reported alterations 'more than twice as common'. Studies may add paired evidence that the alteration is absent before treatment and present at progression. When only a minority of patients show the change, a control is needed that gives the background rate of the same change: paired samples without the drug, or without resistance. For HER2 this background is large. Niikura 2012 found 24% of HER2+ primaries had HER2- metastases, and trastuzumab exposure did not significantly change this rate (P=0.296). A few recurrent events with no control therefore do not establish association. Ignatov 2019 is the exception: it did find HER2 loss linked to anti-HER2 therapy versus a control group. HOW SURE: medium. SOURCES: https://www.cell.com/cancer-cell/fulltext/S1535-6108(18)30368-4, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3295557/, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30806922/.

question: FINDING FROM THE LAB'S LIBRARY, asked for by the director. QUESTION: What is the typical rate of discordance in targeted-panel ERBB2 amplification calls between two biopsies of the same untreated tumour (primary vs. metastasis, or different regions), and what tumour purity is needed for reliable panel-based ERBB2 amplification calling? ANSWER: Pooled HER2 discordance between primary and metastasis is about 8-10% (meta-analyses: 8% across 48 studies, 10.3% across 39 studies), with positive-to-negative conversion in about 21% of HER2+ primaries. Single-centre studies give about 24% HER2+ to HER2- (Niikura 2012), not significantly affected by trastuzumab. These figures are from IHC/FISH; no panel-NGS rate for untreated paired samples was found, so the web does not fully settle the panel-specific rate. For purity, MSK-IMPACT ERBB2 calls were 98.4% concordant with IHC/FISH, and the discordant calls came from low tumour content or HER2 heterogeneity. Amplicon NGS loses sensitivity for amplification below about 30% cellularity (Oncomine validation). Treat non-amplified calls in samples under ~30% purity as unreliable evidence of loss. HOW SURE: medium. SOURCES: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11420314/, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3295557/, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5397722/, https://www.mdpi.com/2072-6694/16/23/3927.

question: FINDING FROM THE LAB'S LIBRARY, asked for by the director. QUESTION: With targeted-panel sequencing data, what evidence is accepted to show that an ERBB2-non-amplified subclone existed before therapy (i.e., selection rather than a de novo change or a sampling artefact)? ANSWER: Showing selection means detecting the resistant (here ERBB2-non-amplified) subclone in the pre-treatment sample. Accepted kinds of evidence are: a subclonal or intermediate ERBB2 copy number at baseline, or HER2 heterogeneity by FISH/IHC; multi-region, deep or single-cell sequencing; and phylogenetic or clonal-mutation evidence placing the post-treatment clone on a branch already present at baseline. The reviews warn that routine clinical assays often miss subclones because of their detection limits and because of sampling. A simple change from amplified to non-amplified between two panel calls therefore cannot distinguish selection from a de novo change or a purity or sampling artefact. The pages read did not give explicit panel-specific criteria, so this is only partly settled. HOW SURE: low. SOURCES: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5528620/, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4838548/, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5397722/.

QUESTION: Under standard somatic-variant interpretation guidelines (AMP/ASCO/CAP, ClinGen/CGC/VICC oncogenicity SOP), what evidence is needed to call a non-hotspot kinase missense variant 'activating', and can genomic patterns alone (mutual exclusivity, recurrence) meet it? OS1 is the same amino acid change as an established oncogenic variant (4). OS3 is a cancerhotspots.org hotspot with at least 50 samples at the position and at least 10 with the same change (4). OM1 is a critical, well-established functional-domain site (2). OM3 is a smaller hotspot (2). OM4 is a different oncogenic missense change at the same residue (2). OP1 is in-silico predictions that all agree (1). OP3 is a hotspot where the same change is seen fewer than 10 times (1). OP4 is absence from gnomAD (1).
